Opening

Let the first slide carry the title.

Slide notes

Use this area for source notes, presenter commentary, or a concise explanation. Readers can click any note area between cards to hide or restore all notes and page gaps, similar to toggling page whitespace in a document editor.

2/15

Cover

A quieter title page.

Use this when the deck opens with a precise topic rather than a logo or image.

Slide notes

A text-first cover works for analytical, research, policy, academic, and internal readouts where clarity matters more than spectacle.

3/15
Section

A section can reset the rhythm.

02

Use dark or high-contrast covers sparingly for chapter breaks and major transitions.

Slide notes

Section covers help long decks breathe, especially when moving from setup to evidence or from diagnosis to action.

4/15
Evidence

A clear claim plus a concrete image.

Use split layouts for people, products, places, launches, screenshots, and artifacts.

Slide notes

Replace the placeholder path with a real source-backed image, screenshot, or generated raster asset. Use fit-contain when details matter more than crop.

5/15
Full-bleed source-backed image
Photo Cover

Let a real image establish the subject.

Use this when the person, product, place, or event should be visible before explanation.

Slide notes

Use source-backed photos or screenshots for real products, people, places, events, and news. Keep overlay text short and high contrast.

6/15
Image Row

Use image rows for before/after states, product variants, screenshots, or visual evidence that should be compared at equal scale.

Slide notes

Keep all images in the same ratio and use captions for provenance, caveats, and the interpretation that connects the set.

7/15

Screenshot detail

Screenshots need room for inspection.

Use a wider media slot when UI details, labels, or product states are the evidence.

  • Best for product audits, launch recaps, interface comparisons, and artifact reading.
  • Move source notes and caveats into the caption so the visual can stay large.
Slide notes

Prefer fit-contain for screenshots with small text. Add callouts only when they identify real visual evidence.

8/15
KPI Summary

Efficiency improved, but the gain is concentrated in two channels.

Use KPI summary when the headline judgment matters more than one specific chart.

Revenue 776.8k +14% vs prior period
ROAS 1.88x June recovered to 2.01x
Spend 412.2k May carried the scale-up
Slide notes

KPI cards should carry reviewed values, clear units, and short interpretation. Put source definitions and caveats here.

11/15
Dense Reading

Use a reading layout when the explanation itself is the artifact.

Some slides need more than a headline and three labels. A reading page gives the main explanation a comfortable line length, while the sidebar holds terms, dates, source notes, or decision criteria.

This is useful for research synthesis, teaching material, policy context, project rationale, and any moment where the audience should be able to understand the point without presenter narration.

Sidebar

  • Keep definitions near the body text.
  • Use captions for sources and caveats.
  • Split the slide when the body needs a second claim.
Slide notes

Dense reading pages are for real explanation, not decorative filler. They should still carry one clear idea.

12/15
Argument

A stronger claim belongs above the proof, not beside every detail.

Evidence

Use one concrete observation, source excerpt, metric, or example. It should be specific enough to verify without becoming a paragraph dump.

Mechanism

Explain why the evidence matters. This slot is where causality, constraint, incentive, or user behavior becomes explicit.

Implication

Close with the consequence: a decision, a risk, a next step, or the question that should shape the following slide.

Slide notes

Use argument grids for recommendations, research findings, strategy decisions, and short synthesis pages.

13/15
Comparison

Compare alternatives on the same dimensions.

Option A

  • Goal: maximize speed and reduce first-pass complexity.
  • Tool: focus scope around the highest-confidence decision path.
  • Risk: misses edge cases that matter to later implementation.

Option B

  • Goal: maximize coverage and expose hidden tradeoffs early.
  • Tool: compare more dimensions with consistent wording.
  • Risk: slows the read and weakens the headline decision.
Slide notes

Use comparison pages for before/after, policy choices, product alternatives, operating models, and scenario tradeoffs.

14/15
Timeline

A sequence should show consequence, not only order.

1. Trigger

Name the condition that changed and made the next move possible.

2. Decision

State who acted, what they chose, and what constraint shaped the choice.

3. Effect

Show the immediate shift in behavior, economics, policy, or system state.

4. Residue

Close with what remained unresolved and why it matters now.

Slide notes

Use timeline and chain layouts for causal explanations, launches, incident reviews, history, and process narratives.

15/15
Takeaway

One card, one idea.

15

Use notes for the rest.

Slide notes

Caption text can be longer than slide text. It should add useful context rather than repeating the headline.
